pages.text: 2026 marked year of growth for AUSL Skip to Content The second season of the Athletes Unlimited Softball League concluded over the weekend, with the Utah Talons and superstar pitcher Montana Fouts repeating as league champions . However, that hardly signals that things were the same in the AUSL in 2026 as they were a year ago. The league added two expansion teams (Portland and Oklahoma City), played in dedicated markets for the first time, saw widespread increases in fan interest and made history in softball broadcasting. Commissioner Kim Ng acknowledged the league needed to “prove” itself when it began 15 months ago. Those things helped do just that, in addition to capitalizing on a general “thirst” for softball fans over the past few years. A thrilling season on the field with several breakout stars helped, too. “I think, quite convincingly, we are bringing on more fans who have not really even seen the game of softball,” Ng said in a postseason press conference Wednesday. “So really happy about those moments.” ATHLETES UNLIMITED SOFTBALL LEAGUE Talons win second straight AUSL title Everything to know about AUSL All-Star Cup Complete AUSL coverage Jon Patricof, CEO and co-founder of Athletes Unlimited, said Game 1 of the 2026 AUSL Championship Series -- which aired on ABC -- was the first ever professional softball game on broadcast television. pages.text: 2027 Women's World Cup: Northern Ireland and Republic of Ireland learn play-off routes - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images/Press Eye Image caption, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland both face tricky play-off ties in their bid to reach the World Cup By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 18 June 2026 Northern Ireland face a difficult 2027 Women's World Cup play-off with Portugal, while the Republic of Ireland will take on Kazakhstan. Michael McArdle's side will be underdogs against Portugal, who beat NI twice in Euro 2025 qualifying. If they can win that game, then either Iceland or Croatia await in the second round of play-offs. Given their play-off ranking, even if Northern Ireland could stun two of Europe's biggest sides they could still face an additional inter-continental play-off to make it to the finals in Brazil. The Republic of Ireland, who qualified for a first World Cup in 2023, will face a first round tie with Kazakhstan. If Carla Ward's side progress, then they will face either Belgium or Poland in a bid to reach the finals. The first round ties will take place in October, while the second play-off round is scheduled for the international window in November and December. pages.title: 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed : NPR
pages.description: In one family, three generations of American women explore how choices around becoming mothers have changed at the same time the U.S. birth rate has dropped.
pages.text: 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player 3 generations of women show how choices on having kids changed In one family, three generations of American women explore how choices around becoming mothers have changed at the same time the U.S. birth rate has dropped. 3 generations of women in one family show how choices on motherhood have changed January 28, 2026 5:00 AM ET By Sarah McCammon , Avery Keatley Caroline Brown (left) and Cynthia Briscoe Brown look at family photo album with their grandmother and mother Barbara Briscoe (seated) in Atlanta. Nicole Buchanan for NPR hide caption toggle caption i Nicole Buchanan for NPR American women today are having fewer children than their mothers and grandmothers did. They also have more opportunities and life choices. "I don't really feel like I got strong messages about what my life should look like beyond college graduation," said Caroline Brown, 33, of Charlotte, N.C.. "I was very much under the impression that the world was kind of my oyster." Like a growing number of younger women, she's unsure if she wants children. And she's not unusual; the U.S. birthrate now is about half of what it was in the 1960s. Caroline's grandmother, Barbara Briscoe, 93, says during her childbearing years, there wasn't a big question about what she was going to do with her life.
